replying_to: Replying to Poly-CAM: High resolution class activation map for convolutional neural networks
display_title: Official Review of Paper2650 by Reviewer 6Awa

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new method, Poly-CAM, to produce high resolution class activation maps without gradient backpropagation. The proposed method gradually upsamples the activation maps from the deeper layers and uses them to weigh the activation maps in the shallower layers. The proposed method also studies three different weighting methods.
content.main_review:
+The proposed method is motivated well.
+The experiments seem convincing and the performance is impressive.
+The analysis in this paper is good.
+The paper is easy to read and follow.

-I have to say that I am not the expert in this area. While I find the proposed method is effective, I feel that the main idea of fusing multi-layer activation maps is not very exciting. The intuition behind the ``Channel-wise Decrease of Confidence'' is also straightforward.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I think it is a good submssion, as the proposed method seems effective and the analysis is good. However, I feel that the idea is somewhat incremental. Fusion is not an exciting idea to me. But I am not the expert in this area, so I am open to hear from other reviewers and the authors.

###############################################################
I thank the authors for their replies and additional experiments. In the initial stage, I found the proposed idea of fusing multi-layer activation maps not significant. As other reviewers pointed out, this idea has been explored before. I did not find a high-level discussion that explains the differences between the proposed idea and the idea in the published paper.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2650 by Reviewer 6Awa

content.title: Reply to Reviewer 6Awa
content.comment: Thank you for your positive comments. The main revisions listed in the ‘reply to all reviewers’ above confirm that, while simple in principle, our proposed Poly-CAM method provides a quite relevant manner to combine the multiple activation maps associated to the layers of a CNN. It results in saliency maps that achieve unprecedent level of accuracy (see Fig. 5) and robustness (see the sensitivity analysis in Table 5, Appendix F). Moreover, the ablation study that is now provided in Appendix B, demonstrates the importance of (i) combining multiple layers; and (ii) doing it based on Equation (3), without omitting the LNorm operator. Comparisons between Poly-CAM and very recent works addressing the same problem, i.e.  Zoom-CAM (ICPR 2021) and Layer-CAM (IEEE Transactions on Image Processing 2021), are in favor of our proposed method. This positions our work as the new reference solution for class-specific saliency map visualizations.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2650 by Reviewer 6Awa

content.title: Reply the additional comment from 6Awa
content.comment:
The modification introduced today by reviewer ‘6Awa’ sounds light and unfounded.

In particular, the reduction of the grade from 6 to 5 sounds unjustified, since it is based on incorrect arguments.

Our revisions and replies to each of the initial comments from reviewers both complete/clarify the manuscript and confirm the superiority (by a large margin in terms of visual assessment) of our approach compared to earlier works in the field (including the very recent ones we had missed in our initial draft).  

Hence, they all reinforce our contribution.

We hope those replies, and the added value the reviewers could bring to our paper through their comments, will be considered seriously by the AC and other reviewers, despite this unexpected repositioning of reviewer ‘6Awa’.
 
We indeed respectfully disagree with the specific arguments (incomplete positioning with earlier methods, and lack of novelty) raised by reviewer ‘6Awa’ since:

The way our approach differs from earlier attempts to merge activation maps has been clarified in the revised version, both through the inclusion of Fig.1, and the clarifications of the mathematical description provided by Equation (3). Hopefully, it is now clear that the core idea underlying our approach lies in the local tuning of the upsampled version of the saliency map provided by subsequent layers. In contrast, as now told in the related work section, methods like Zoom-CAM and Layer-CAM build on gradients to increase the resolution of saliency computed in the different layers of the network.
This difference is shown to dramatically impact the quality and resolution of the saliency map.
Extensive comparisons (in Fig. 3 and 5, but also through the 2000 images made available through the Jupiter notebook provided in the zip supplementary material)  are provided to differentiate our proposed approach from earlier attempts to combine multiple layers. All those comparisons are (largely) in favor of our proposal, which confirms the relevance (and novelty) of the proposed approach. It is thus incorrect to point the lack of novelty as an issue for our paper.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2650 by Reviewer aZq6

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper is about visual explanations and builds on top of gradCam. The paper makes the correct observation that gradCam is low resolution. The paper proposes to add intermediate featuremap activations to retain the high-resolution information. Experimental results and visualizations demonstrate that the method can keep more information than considered baselines.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

- Easy to read and understand
- Intuitive idea
- Results look promising

Weaknesses:

- Very similar work on high resolution class activation maps is missed, see missing ref [a] below.
- Bit sloppy in equations, see details below.

Missing citation:

[a] Shi et al "Zoom-CAM: Generating Fine-grained Pixel Annotations from Image Labels" In International Conference on Pattern Recognition (ICPR), 2020

The missing citation [a] uses exactly the same idea of exploiting the activations of intermediate layers to generate high-resolution visualizations. Thus, the "novelty" claims in this ICLR submission seem not so strong.

Sure, the exact approach is slightly different than [a], but I would expect:
- a conceptual comparison of how this ICLR submission is different in related work
- an experimental comparison to demonstrate the empirical difference 

Some details:

- Eq 1: what is the min or max of a matrix? Is it a scalar? Then you subtract a scalar from a matrix (which is technically not possible, as only matrices of the same size can be subtracted), so I assume it is all done element wise? (ie: the scalar is 'broadcasted' to be of the same size as the matrix? It would be good to make this explicit.

- Eq 4: the term \bf{w} is not defined. I assume these are the learnable parameters in each layer l? I think these are called \Theta, earlier, which is confusing. It would be good to make this explicit.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea is sound but there is a very similar unreferenced published paper [a]. Without a conceptual and empirical comparison to [a] I cannot accept this paper.

replying_to: Replying to Poly-CAM: High resolution class activation map for convolutional neural networks
display_title: Official Review of Paper2650 by Reviewer BXML

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors proposed a new XAI method, named POLY-CAM, to extend classic Grad-CAM to generate high resolution class activation maps, without relying on gradient backpropagation. Briefly speaking, POLY-CAM is achieved by aggregating the activation maps from the early layers to the last layers instead of sticking to the last layer only. POLY-CAM shows the state-of-the-art performance in terms of faithfulness metric, and unsurprisingly passes the sanity check.
content.main_review:
1.	The largest claimed contribution of the paper is using activation maps from multiple layers instead of the last layer. It’s not surprising that the earlier layer activation map you use, the higher resolution you can possibly get, and thus the subtle relationship you can better obtain. An immediate question naturally arise is the good performance due to the usage of the first layer or it’s due to the mixture of different layers. The author should at least list the activation map w.r.t each single layer as baselines, using the 3 weights mentioned in the paper. 
2.	According to my understanding, the XAI method can only achieve a tradeoff between resolution and robustness. For example, Grad-CAM is low resolution but robust whereas saliency methods are the opposite. Since POLY-CAM resembles more to the saliency methods, the author should at least choose some classic saliency methods such as SmoothGrad and Integrated Gradient as baselines too. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis is needed to demonstrate to what extent POLY-CAM is robust to the adversarial attack.
3.	The insertion and deletion faithfulness metric has an intrinsic problem in the sense that the inserted/deleted image is most likely out-of-distribution. That being said, the change of class softmax output can be ill-behaved and not really trustworthy. How to justify this?
4.	How is P_L^c is defined in Eq. (4)? 
5.	How is  s_l set? The closer to the input the larger? If so, it implies that maybe the activation map from the first layer can suffice.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper aims to tackle the interesting XAI problem. It’s well-written, easy to follow, and the literature review is quite comprehensive. However, the questions need to be addressed to my concern of the novelty.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2650 by Reviewer BXML

content.title: Reply to Reviewer BXML
content.comment:
Thank you for the clarity and constructiveness of your comments.  

Most of them have motivated the main revisions listed in the ‘reply to all reviewers’ provided above. They include the clarification of Equation (3) and Fig. 1, a careful investigation of the advantage brought by the merging of multiple maps (see Section B in Appendix), the comparison to gradient-based methods (Section 4 and Appendix E), and a sensitivity analysis (see Appendix F). In particular, the combination of the results presented in Figure 5 (visual assessment) and Table 5 (sensitivity analysis) reveals that our Poly-CAM method reaches an unprecedently good trade-off between resolution and robustness. This emphasizes the value of Poly-CAM, since it provides a saliency map that contradicts the idea that robustness and resolution are antagonistic goals. 

Regarding the relevance of insertion/deletion metrics, we fully agree with the reviewer’s opinion. Even with a blurred baseline, masked images tend to be outliers. Those metrics are definitely arguable, but currently correspond to the best (most widely spread) alternative for a quantitative assessment of the maps. However, those metrics should never be considered blindly, and a qualitative visual assessment should remain the golden standard to evaluate saliency maps. Our revised paper now explicitly mentions that the metrics outcome should be considered with caution (see Section 4.2.1)

replying_to: Replying to Poly-CAM: High resolution class activation map for convolutional neural networks
display_title: Official Review of Paper2650 by Reviewer 1byE

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces a new CAM-based method called Poly-CAM, which aims to generate high-resolution maps.  In particular, it proposes to utilize activation maps (in higher resolution) from earlier layers via a local normalization (LNorm) operator, and contribute a way to compute the weight in CAMs. The author claims this method achieve the state-of-art performance on corresponding metrics for explaining network prediction.
content.main_review:
Pros: 
+ Explainability of neural networks is an important research topic and highly relevant to ICLR audience.
+ This work aims to solve an inherited problem (low resolution) existed in previous CAMs.
+ For the definition of weight, this work build on the top of CIC from Score-CAM and introduce two extensions, CDC and CVC.
+ It achieves a better performance on insertion and deletion metrics.

Cons: 
- The paper is not well written and hard to follow. For example, the notations are messy (in section 3.1). The notation is not consistent (use L in 3.2, while use l in 3.3). For the core equation (4), what is the definition of P^c_l? It only shows the recursive step without the final result like equation (3).
- The reason for using LNorm is not clear enough. Why it works? Or is it necessary? If I understand correctly, it measures the distortion of pooling and upsampling, but what kind of role does it play in (4)? More explanations are needed before I consider increasing my score.
- The insertion-deletion difference metric cannot be regarded as a new metric, it is just a subtraction without any information gain.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I vote for rejecting, with lots of concerns unsolved. 

I like the recursive approach that backpropagate the weight from final layer to earlier layers so that the generated map is in high resolution. My major concern is about the clarity of the paper and additional explanations for key operations. I can increase my score if the authors can address my concern in the rebuttal period.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2650 by Reviewer 1byE

content.title: Reply to Reviewer 1byE
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback. Your comments largely contributed to the main revisions listed in the ‘reply to all reviewers’. They include clarification of the method description (see revisions associated to Fig. 1 and Eq. (3) ), motivation of LNorm (see Section B.2 in Supplementary), and deeper experimental study, including sensitivity analysis, comparison of Poly-CAM strategy with naive CAM layers fusion, and comparison with Zoom-CAM and Layer-CAM.  

Hopefully, those revisions also clarify the novelty and contribution significance issues. The novelty primary lies in the definition of Equation (3), and the definition of CDC and CVC has to be considered as a secondary incremental contribution.  This has now been clarified in the introduction of the paper. Moreover, from the extensive experiments we have conducted, the Poly-CAM strategy depicted in Fig. 1 appears to improve the saliency map accuracy by a large margin (see Fig. 3 and 5), with a potentially critical impact in terms of explainability (see the example presented in Fig. 17 (Appendix D.2), where CAM is unable to convince the medical doctor that the model is relevant, while Poly-CAM tends to show that the model works fine)

content.title: Response to Author
content.comment:
Thanks for reply. Although the revised version provides further explanation of LNorm in Sec 3.3 and ablation study in Appendix, some of my concerns still remain unsolved.

First, it is not clear to me why "LNorm ensures that an image block with large saliency in layer l+1 has also a large saliency in layer l". The LNorm only works on layer l, how it connects to l+1?

Second, as I mentioned before, LNorm seems to measure the distortion of pooling and upsampling (please correct me if I misunderstand), what is the meaning of the value in the map after LNorm? Besides, is there any visualization result of original map at layer l and its counterpart after LNorm? How about their difference?

content.title: Response to reviewer 1byE
content.comment:
Here are the replies to your question.

Regarding the first question, note that the important part in the sentence ‘It ensures that an image block with large saliency in layer l+1 has also a large saliency in layer l, even if the level of activation in this block is small compared to the rest of the image.’ is actually ‘even if the level of activation in this block is small compared to the rest of the image’. In other words, in cases where the activations in layer l are spatially quite heterogeneous, applying LNorm avoids that the spatial region with the highest activation values in layer l becomes the only salient region in the saliency map corresponding to this layer.

Regarding the second question, as told above, LNorm really aims at putting all spatial regions on an equal footing, regardless the mean intensity of the region activations. This is because, our purpose it to use the activation pattern in layer l to locally tune/modulate the smooth saliency map provided by layer l+1.

To clarify how LNorm is affecting the CAM map of layer l, we have now added the map obtained after LNorm in Fig. 1. We observe that LNorm flattens the global variations of CAM, while preserving its local (and high frequency) fluctuations.

To illustrate the importance of LNorm, the ablation study in appendix B2 provides examples of saliency maps that have been computed with and without LNorm. More examples (2000 images from ImageNet) of saliency maps computed without LNorm are now available through the Jupiter notebook interface in "interactive_saliency_visualization.ipynb" (see the zip file associated to submission). You need to uncomment line associated to the ablation study in the "Saliency selection" section and to download the suplementary saliency maps from the associated wedsite https://polycam.ddns.net.

content.title: Response to Author
content.comment: The feedback solves part of my concerns. I can increase my score with +1. But overall, I think this paper is not ready to be accepted.

replying_to: Replying to Poly-CAM: High resolution class activation map for convolutional neural networks
display_title: Reply to all reviewers and AC

content.title: Reply to all reviewers and AC
content.comment:
Thank you for your replies.

All reviewers did align on a note of 5, i.e on a polite rejection of the paper. This decision seems to be motivated by a lack of novelty.

We have to admit this argument sounds weird to us.

Several previous works (including the authors of Grad-CAM who tried without success on the earlier layers, as attested by a footnote in their paper) have indeed considered the exploitation of earlier activation layers to identify the salient features exploited by the network.
Hence, we fully agree on the fact that there is no creativity in the use of multiple activation maps to derive a precise & relevant saliency map.

However, the mixed results obtained by those previous approaches (including the very recent ones missed in our initial submission) demonstrate that the devil lies in the details. In that context, our contribution should not be associated to the idea of combining  maps, but to the way this combination is implemented.

On that aspect, the novelty is undeniable: none of the previous works that proposed to combine activation maps from multiple layers was able to achieve the level of details provided by our approach (just look at the comparison provided in Figure 3 and/or Figure 5... the difference is simply amazing). In an industrial context, often working with images at low resolution, reaching this level of details makes a huge difference, e.g. to convince a client that a model is working properly.

Overall, we remain convinced that our paper conveys a valuable message, that is of general interest to the community, with a potentially significant impact in terms of practical application. (Thereby, differenciating our contribution from "yet another paper about CAM".)

Does the material provided in the submission leaves any doubt about the fact that our contribution is relevant and without precedent in term of saliency sharpeness?

This is THE question to address in our case. The presentation of significant achievements related to DNNs is indeed one the main reasons that led to the creation of ICLR.
ICLR is a worth attending conference because, through a traditionally solid openreview procedure, it has been able to offer visibility to achievements that make a difference in real life. This is in contrast with some other venues that tend to limit the scientific exchange to mathematically sound contributions, thereby ignoring many insightful experimental studies involving DNNs.
